title: return, not repentance
hookLine: return, not repentance — you're not lost, you're facing the wrong way

cards: You're driving somewhere new, and you miss the exit. The map on your phone doesn't lecture you. It doesn't tell you you're a bad driver or that you've ruined the trip.
It just says: recalculating. And then, somewhere up ahead: make a U-turn. You were never lost, exactly.
You were going the wrong way, and the way back was always there. English has a heavy word for what happens after we do wrong: repentance. It sounds like sackcloth and shame.
The Hebrew word underneath it is much closer to that voice on the map. Today: teshuvah.

teach.b: Teshuvah comes from shuv, to turn, to return. It doesn't say you're broken. It says you're facing the wrong way, and you can turn around.
The prophet Hosea calls out: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God." Return. As if home were still there.
The same Hebrew word also means an answer, a reply. Turning around is answering a call.

The rabbis thought teshuvah was so basic to the world that they listed it among the things created before the world itself, before anyone had done anything wrong. The way back was built before the road.
So how does a person actually turn? Maimonides lays it out plainly.
Stop doing the thing. Regret it, honestly. Say it out loud, in words, not just in your head.

And decide not to do it again. Then his test for complete teshuvah: you find yourself in the same situation, with the same temptation and the same strength, and this time you don't do it. Not because you can't.
Because you've turned. Two bold teachings go further.

teach.h: WHERE THE ONE WHO RETURNS STANDS.
teach.b: One rabbi says: in the place where a person who has returned stands, even the completely righteous cannot stand.

The one who turned has walked a road the others never had to walk. And another says that when teshuvah comes from love, even deliberate wrongs are turned into merits, as if the wrong turn became part of the way home.
The month before the new year, and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, are set aside for exactly this. But tradition doesn't lock the door the rest of the year. It holds it open any day.

how: Jews focus on teshuvah especially in the month of Elul and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, reflecting on the year, apologizing to people they've wronged and resolving to change, though tradition holds it's possible any day.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: it means turning: you're facing the wrong way, and you can turn around.
the rabbis listed teshuvah among things made before the world
the way back was built before anyone went wrong.
teshuvah is only possible around Yom Kippur
the autumn is set aside for it, but the door is open any day.

games.q: a year later you're in the same situation, same temptation, same strength. by Maimonides' test, what makes it complete teshuvah?
o: you don't do it, though you could.
games.why: complete teshuvah: same place, same strength, and this time you don't do it, because you've turned.

practice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. If you can, stand up and slowly turn around, all the way, so you're facing the other side of the room. Then sit.
Bring to mind one habit or direction in your life that's pointing the wrong way. Not a verdict on yourself. Just the direction.
Picture the U-turn. If you pray, you can ask for help turning.

wordCard.voice: Teshuvah. Return: not shame, but turning around, and answering the call home. Nineteenth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: return, from shuv, to turn. it also means an answer.

carryVoice: Your line: turn around. No shame required, only the U-turn, one at a time. Day nineteen, done.
